results.title: Measurement Invariance: Complete Guide to Cross-Group Test Validity | Cogn-IQ
results.content: Reviewed by: Xavier Jouve, Ph.D. Measurement invariance is the statistical property ensuring that a test measures the same construct across different groups, times, or conditions. Measurement invariance, also known as measurement equivalence, is a fundamental psychometric property that determines whether a test measures the same construct in the same way across different groups, occasions, or conditions. * Learn methods for testing invariance using confirmatory factor analysis. The most common approach to testing measurement invariance involves multi-group confirmatory factor analysis (MG-CFA). Invariance testing is fundamental to ensuring test fairness across demographic groups. Violations of measurement invariance indicate potential test bias, where individuals from different groups with equal ability levels receive different scores. Effect sizes for non-invariance, such as dMACS for mean differences or R-square changes, provide practical significance beyond statistical tests. Recent methodological advances include approximate measurement invariance using Bayesian methods, alignment optimization for many groups, and moderated nonlinear factor analysis for continuous moderators. Measurement invariance testing is essential for ethical test use but requires expertise in psychometric methods.

results.content: Despite the controversy over the concept of test fairness, numerous empirical studies have been carried out to investigate various aspects of test fairness, including item-level analyses of differential item functioning (DIF) across different latent (e.g., Aryadoust, 2018;Aryadoust & Zhang, 2016;Chen & Jiao, 2014;Oliveri, Ercikan, Lyons-Thomas, & Holtzman, 2016) or manifest subgroups (e.g., Cadime, Viana, & Ribeiro, 2014;Elder, 1996;Kim, 2001;Pae, 2004aPae, , 2004bPae, , 2012 Pae & Park, 2006;Ryan & Bachman, 1992) and test-level investigations of the invariance of factor structures of the test across different subgroups (e.g., Kunnan, 1994;Stricker, Rock, & Lee, 2005;Yoo & Manna, 2017), shedding light on how psychometric methods based on classical test theory (CTT) and item response theory (IRT) can be incorporated in the investigations of fairness of language tests.
